statement: If in a circle which has its diameter rational an equilateral pentagon be inscribed, the side of the pentagon is the irrational straight line called minor.
heath_proof: For in the circle ABCDE which has its diameter rational let the equilateral pentagon ABCDE be inscribed; I say that the side of the pentagon is the irrational straight line called minor. For let the centre of the circle, the point F, be taken, let AF, FB be joined and carried through to the points, G, H, let AC be joined, and let FK be made a fourth part of AF. Now AF is rational; therefore FK is also rational. But BF is also rational; therefore the whole BK is rational. And, since the circumference ACG is equal to the circumference ADG, and in them ABC is equal to AED, therefore the remainder CG is equal to the remainder GD. And, if we join AD, we conclude that the angles at L are right, and CD is double of CL. For the same reason the angles at M are also right, and AC is double of CM. Since then the angle ALC is equal to the angle AMF, and the angle LAC is common to the two triangles ACL and AMF, therefore the remaining angle ACL is equal to the remaining angle MFA; [I. 32] therefore the triangle ACL is equiangular with the triangle AMF; therefore, proportionally, as LC is to CA, so is MF to FA. And the doubles of the antecedents may be taken; therefore, as the double of LC is to CA, so is the double of MF to FA. But, as the double of MF is to FA, so is MF to the half of FA; therefore also, as the double of LC is to CA, so is MF to the half of FA. And the halves of the consequents may be taken; therefore, as the double of LC is to the half of CA, so is MF to the fourth of FA. And DC is double of LC, CM is half of CA, and FK a fourth part of FA; therefore, as DC is to CM, so is MF to FK. Componendo also, as the sum of DC, CM is to CM, so is MK to KF; [V. 18] therefore also, as the square on the sum of DC, CM is to the square on CM, so is the square on MK to the square on KF. And since, when the straight line subtending two sides of the pentagon, as AC, is cut in extreme and mean ratio, the greater segment is equal to the side of the pentagon, that is, to DC, [XIII. 8] while the square on the greater segment added to the half of the whole is five times the square on the half of the whole, [XIII. 1] and CM is half of the whole AC, therefore the square on DC, CM taken as one straight line is five times the square on CM. But it was proved that, as the square on DC, CM taken as one straight line is to the square on CM, so is the square on MK to the square on KF; therefore the square on MK is five times the square on KF. But the square on KF is rational, for the diameter is rational; therefore the square on MK is also rational; therefore MK is rational And, since BF is quadruple of FK, therefore BK is five times KF; therefore the square on BK is twenty-five times the square on KF. But the square on MK is five times the square on KF; therefore the square on BK is five times the square on KM; therefore the square on BK has not to the square on KM the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore BK is incommensurable in length with KM. [X. 9] And each of them is rational. Therefore BK, KM are rational straight lines commensurable in square only. But, if from a rational straight line there be subtracted a rational straight line which is commensurable with the whole in square only, the remainder is irrational, namely an apotome; therefore MB is an apotome and MK the annex to it. [X. 73] I say next that MB is also a fourth apotome. Let the square on N be equal to that by which the square on BK is greater than the square on KM; therefore the square on BK is greater than the square on KM by the square on N. And, since KF is commensurable with FB, componendo also, KB is commensurable with FB. [X. 15] But BF is commensurable with BH; therefore BK is also commensurable with BH. [X. 12] And, since the square on BK is five times the square on KM, therefore the square on BK has to the square on KM the ratio which 5 has to 1. Therefore, convertendo, the square on BK has to the square on N the ratio which 5 has to 4 [V. 19], and this is not the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore BK is incommensurable with N; [X. 9] therefore the square on BK is greater than the square on KM by the square on a straight line incommensurable with BK. Since then the square on the whole BK is greater than the square on the annex KM by the square on a straight line incommensurable with BK, and the whole BK is commensurable with the rational straight line, BH, set out, therefore MB is a fourth apotome. [X. Deff. III. 4] But the rectangle contained by a rational straight line and a fourth apotome is irrational, and its square root is irrational, and is called minor. [X. 94] But the square on AB is equal to the rectangle HB, BM, because, when AH is joined, the triangle ABH is equiangular with the triangle ABM, and, as HB is to BA, so is AB to BM. Therefore the side AB of the pentagon is the irrational straight line called minor.
ai_proof_text:
13.11
**Statement:** If in a circle which has its diameter rational an equilateral pentagon be inscribed, the side of the pentagon is the irrational straight line called minor.

**Step 1.** Let ABCDE be a circle whose diameter is rational, and let the equilateral pentagon ABCDE be inscribed in it, so that AB = BC = CD = DE = EA. Take the centre F of the circle (3.1). Join AF and BF (P1) and produce them to meet the circumference again at G and H respectively (P2); AG and BH are then diameters (D1.17). Join AC and BD (P1). Since FA = FB = FG = FH, being radii (D1.15), BH is double of BF and AG is double of AF. Bisect AF, and bisect the half again (1.10), so obtaining a fourth part of AF; on FH cut off FK equal to this fourth part (1.3). Then FA = FB = 4FK, BK = BF + FK = 5FK, BH = 2BF = 8FK, and K lies between F and H.

**Step 2.** Since the diameter is rational, take the diameter BH as the rational straight line set out. FK measures BH (BH = 8FK), and likewise measures FA, FB and BK; so each of FK, FA, FB, BK is commensurable in length with BH (D10.1.1) and is therefore rational (D10.1.3). Further, KF being commensurable in length with BH, the square on KF has to the square on BH the ratio which a square number has to a square number (10.9), so these squares are commensurable (10.6); hence the square on KF is rational (D10.1.4).

**Step 3.** Since the straight lines AB, BC, CD, DE, EA are equal, they cut off equal circumferences (3.28); so the arcs AB, BC, CD, DE, EA are equal. Hence the arc ABC (= arcs AB + BC) is equal to the arc AED (= arcs AE + ED) (CN2), and therefore the chord AC is equal to the chord AD (3.29). Again, the angle EAB stands on the arc BCDE, the angle ABC on the arc CDEA, and similarly for the other angles; each of these arcs is made up of three of the five equal arcs, so they are all equal (CN2), and hence the five angles of the pentagon are equal (3.27). Thus the pentagon ABCDE is both equilateral and equiangular.

**Step 4.** In the triangles ABF, CBF, AB = CB, BF is common, and FA = FC (D1.15); therefore the angle ABF is equal to the angle CBF (1.8). So BF lies within the angle ABC and meets AC; let it meet AC at M. (M lies between B and F, because the arc ABC, being two of the five equal arcs, is less than a semicircle, so that the centre F lies on the side of AC remote from B.) In the triangles ABM, CBM, AB = CB, BM is common, and the angle ABM is equal to the angle CBM; therefore AM = MC and the angle AMB is equal to the angle CMB (1.4), so each of them is right (D1.10). Thus CA = 2CM, and CM is perpendicular to BH at M. On the line BH the points lie in the order B, M, F, K, H; hence BK = BM + MK and MK = MF + FK.

**Step 5.** In the triangles CAF, DAF, CA = DA (Step 3), AF is common, and FC = FD (D1.15); therefore the angle CAF is equal to the angle DAF (1.8). So AF produced, that is AG, lies within the angle CAD and meets CD; let it meet CD at L. In the triangles CAL, DAL, CA = DA, AL is common, and the angle CAL is equal to the angle DAL; therefore CL = LD and the angle ALC is equal to the angle ALD (1.4), so each of them is right (D1.10). Thus DC = 2CL.

**Step 6.** Consider the triangles ACL, AFM. The angle ALC is equal to the angle AMF, both being right (P4); and the angle CAL is the same angle as the angle FAM, since L lies on AF produced and M lies on AC. Therefore the remaining angle ACL is equal to the remaining angle AFM (1.32), and the triangles ACL, AFM are equiangular. Hence the sides about the equal angles are proportional, those sides corresponding which subtend equal angles (6.4): as CL is to CA, so is FM to FA (CA and FA subtending the right angles, CL and FM subtending the equal angles at A).

**Step 7.** Alternately (5.16), CL : FM = CA : FA. Now CL : FM = 2CL : 2FM = DC : 2FM (5.15, since DC = 2CL); and CA : FA = 2CM : 4FK = CM : 2FK (5.15, since CA = 2CM and FA = 4FK). Therefore DC : 2FM = CM : 2FK (5.11). Alternately (5.16), DC : CM = 2FM : 2FK; and 2FM : 2FK = FM : FK (5.15). Therefore DC : CM = FM : FK (5.11).

**Step 8.** Componendo (5.18), (DC + CM) : CM = (FM + FK) : FK, that is, (DC + CM) : CM = MK : KF, since MK = MF + FK (Step 4). The squares on these four straight lines being similar figures similarly described on them, the square on (DC + CM) is to the square on CM as the square on MK is to the square on KF (6.22).

**Step 9.** Since ABCDE is an equilateral and equiangular pentagon (Step 3), and the straight lines AC, BD subtend the two angles ABC, BCD taken in order, AC and BD cut one another in extreme and mean ratio, and the greater segment of each is equal to the side of the pentagon (13.8). Thus AC is cut in extreme and mean ratio, and its greater segment is equal to the side DC. Therefore the square on the greater segment together with the half of the whole AC, that is, the square on (DC + CM), CM being half of AC, is five times the square on the half CM (13.1): sq(DC + CM) = 5·sq(CM).

**Step 10.** From Steps 8 and 9, sq(MK) : sq(KF) = 5·sq(CM) : sq(CM). Alternately (5.16), sq(MK) : 5·sq(CM) = sq(KF) : sq(CM); and sq(KF) : sq(CM) = 5·sq(KF) : 5·sq(CM) (5.15); therefore sq(MK) : 5·sq(CM) = 5·sq(KF) : 5·sq(CM) (5.11), whence sq(MK) = 5·sq(KF) (5.9).

**Step 11.** Since sq(MK) is five times sq(KF), sq(MK) has to sq(KF) the ratio which the number five has to the unit; therefore sq(MK) is commensurable with sq(KF) (10.6). But sq(KF) is commensurable with sq(BH) (Step 2); therefore sq(MK) is commensurable with sq(BH) (10.12), so that sq(MK) is rational (D10.1.4), MK is commensurable in square with BH (D10.1.2), and MK is rational (D10.1.3).

**Step 12.** Since BK = 5FK, BK has to KF the ratio 5 : 1; the square on BK has to the square on KF the ratio duplicate of this (6.20), namely 25 : 1 (D5.9), so sq(BK) = 25·sq(KF). But sq(MK) = 5·sq(KF) (Step 10); therefore sq(BK) = 5·sq(MK). Hence sq(BK) has to sq(MK) the ratio which the number five has to the unit, so sq(BK) and sq(MK) are commensurable (10.6), i.e. BK and MK are commensurable in square (D10.1.2); but five has not to one the ratio which a square number has to a square number, so BK is incommensurable in length with MK (10.9). Both BK (Step 2) and MK (Step 11) are rational; therefore BK, MK are rational straight lines commensurable in square only. Also BK is greater than MK, MK being a part of BK (CN5).

**Step 13.** Therefore BM, the remainder when the rational straight line MK, commensurable in square only with the whole BK, is subtracted from the rational straight line BK, is an apotome (10.73), BK being its whole and MK its annex.

**Step 14.** Now sq(BK) − sq(MK) = 5·sq(MK) − sq(MK) = 4·sq(MK). This is the square on the double of MK, since the square on the double of MK has to the square on MK the ratio duplicate of 2 : 1 (6.20), namely 4 : 1 (D5.9). And the square on the double of MK has to sq(BK) the ratio 4·sq(MK) : 5·sq(MK), that is 4 : 5, which is not the ratio of a square number to a square number; hence the double of MK is incommensurable in length with BK (10.9). Thus the square on the whole BK is greater than the square on the annex MK by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with BK, and the whole BK is commensurable in length with the rational straight line BH set out (Step 2). Therefore BM is a fourth apotome (D10.3.4).

**Step 15.** Join CH (P1). Since BH is a diameter, the angle BCH, being in a semicircle, is right (3.31). In the right-angled triangle BCH the perpendicular CM has been drawn from the right angle C to the base BH (Step 4), M lying between B and H; therefore BC is a mean proportional between the base BH and the segment BM adjacent to it (6.8): as BH is to BC, so is BC to BM. Hence the rectangle contained by BH, BM is equal to the square on BC (6.17).

**Step 16.** Thus the square on BC is equal to an area contained by the rational straight line BH and the fourth apotome BM. Therefore the "side" of this area, namely BC, is the irrational straight line called minor (10.94). And BC is the side of the pentagon. Therefore, if in a circle which has its diameter rational an equilateral pentagon be inscribed, the side of the pentagon is the irrational straight line called minor. Q.E.D.
